title: Showing your flat
goal: Show a friend round your flat and say where things go
tip: il- means “the”. Before the sun letters t, th, d, dh, r, z, s, sh, ṣ, ṭ, ẓ, l, n it turns into that letter: ish-shigga, id-darīsha. Before the others it stays il-: il-bāb, il-maṭbakh. chī and chidhi both mean “like this”.
grammar: The article il- and the sun letters
dialogue: mashkūr. hādhi ṣ-ṣāla, w il-maṭbakh hnāk
Thanks. This is the living room, and the kitchen's over there.
And the sofa? This way or that way?
Yes, that's good like that. And the TV?
items: the everyday Emirati form; chī walla chī? = this way or that way?
said all over the Gulf and the usual form in Kuwait; Emiratis say both

title: Big or small, new or old
goal: Describe your new flat to a colleague and ask about her new office
tip: Adjectives come after the noun and add -a for a feminine noun: maktab ṣghīr, bināya gadīma. il- on the noun only makes a sentence: il-ghurfa kbīra (the room is big). “The new office” takes il- twice: il-maktab il-yidīd; “your new office” is maktabich il-yidīd.
grammar: Adjectives after the noun; feminine -a; il- on both for “the new …”
dialogue: ما شاء الله، عندك شقة يديدة؟
mā shāʼ allāh, ʿindak shigga yidīda?
Wow, you've got a new flat?
إي، في بناية قديمة في ديرة
ī, fi bināya gadīma fi Dēra
Yes, in an old building in Deira.
And the flat? Big or small?
صغيرة، بس الغرفة كبيرة. ومكتبج اليديد؟
ṣghīra, bas il-ghurfa kbīra. w maktabich il-yidīd?
Small, but the room's big. And your new office?
My office is nice, but the chair's old!
items: feminine: yidīda; you'll see written جديد
feminine: gadīma; for people say kbīr: rayyāl kbīr, an old man
kbīra walla ṣghīra? = big or small?; not the same as wala (not even)

title: Who are these people?
goal: Say who people in a photo are: where they're from and what they're like
tip: For people, plural adjectives end in -īn: ṭayyib → ṭayybīn (kind), zēn → zēnīn, mashghūl → mashghūlīn (busy), imārāti → imārātiyyīn (Emiratis). hādhēla means “these”: hādhēla rabʿi, these are my friends.
dialogue: These are my mates from work.
لا، في إماراتيين وهنود، وأنا بريطاني
la, fī imārātiyyīn w hnūd, w ana brīṭāni
No, there are Emiratis and Indians, and I'm British.
Good. And are the guys nice?
Yes, they're all good guys, but busy.
items: your mates: rabʿak; to a woman: rabʿich
a woman: brīṭāniyya; ana brīṭāni = I'm British
one man: ṭayyib; one woman: ṭayyba
one man: zēn; one woman: zēna
a woman: mashghūla; a group: mashghūlīn
culture: Most people who live in Dubai aren't Emirati, so many offices and shops work in English, and your colleagues may speak other languages at home. Emiratis notice when a foreigner makes the effort to speak their dialect, even a little.

title: This one or that one?
goal: Choose between things in a shop with “this” and “that”
tip: hādha (m.) and hādhi (f.) mean “this”; hādhāk (m.) and hādhīch (f.) mean “that, over there”. With a noun, the noun takes il-: hādha l-gamīṣ, hādhīch is-sāʿa. Alone they mean “this one, that one”: hādhāk ḥilu.
grammar: Demonstratives near and far: hādha, hādhi, hādhāk, hādhīch
dialogue: شو رأيك؟ هذا القميص ولا هذاك؟
shu raʼyak? hādha l-gamīṣ walla hādhāk?
What do you think? This shirt or that one?
مب حلو. بس هذيك الساعة حلوة!
mub ḥilu. bas hādhīch is-sāʿa ḥilwa!
Not nice. But that watch over there is nice!
إي والله، بس غالية. باخذ القميص
ī wallāh, bas ghālya. bākhidh il-gamīṣ
It really is, but it's expensive. I'll take the shirt.
items: masculine: hādhāk; you'll see written هذيج
what do you think? (to a man)
when buying: bākhidh hādha = I'll take this one

title: This time, these days
goal: Help a friend choose a kandura, using “this time”, “this year” and “these days”
tip: hal- is a short “this” or “these” joined to a noun: hal-marra (this time), hal-ayyām (these days). It follows the sun-letter rule: has-sana (this year), hash-shay (this thing).
grammar: hal- + noun: hal-marra, hal-ayyām, has-sana, hash-shay
dialogue: What do you think of this kandura?
حلوة، بس يعني، كل هالشي أبيض!
ḥilwa, bas yaʿni, kill hash-shay abyaẓ!
It's nice, but, I mean, all this stuff is white!
No, these days there are lots of colours.
Really? So what do you want this time?
هالسنة أبي شي ثاني، لون ثاني
has-sana abi shay thāni, lōn thāni
This year I want something different, another colour.
culture: The kandūra is the long robe Emirati men wear, usually white, with a ghitra (headcloth) on top; in winter you'll also see darker colours. Many Emirati women wear a black ʿabāya and a shēla (headscarf). These are culture words: you'll hear them more than you'll need to say them.

title: Checkpoint 1.1: visiting Sēf's family
goal: Visit Sēf's family home with a friend: Umm Sēf's welcome, how-are-you and thanks for a group
tip: To two or more people, -ak and -ich become -kum: shḥālkum?, ḥayyākum allāh, ʿasākum b-khēr. Commands add -u (tfaẓẓalu), and mashkūr becomes mashkūrīn.
dialogue: هلا والله، حياكم الله! شحالكم؟ عساكم بخير؟
hala wallāh, ḥayyākum allāh! shḥālkum? ʿasākum b-khēr?
Hello, welcome, both of you! How are you? All well, I hope?
b-khēr, allāh yḥayyīch. w inti shḥālich?
Fine, God bless you. And how are you?
Fine, thank God, God keep you both. Come in.
Thank you. Here are some sweets for the house.
Thank you both, that's so kind!
items: to one man: shḥālak; to one woman: shḥālich
to one man: ḥayyāk allāh; reply: allāh yḥayyīk, to a woman allāh yḥayyīch
to one man: ʿasāk b-khēr; to one woman: ʿasāch b-khēr
come in / here you go (to a group)
to one man: tfaẓẓal; to one woman: tfaẓẓali
to one man: allāh ysallmak; to one woman: allāh ysallmich
to one man: mashkūr; to one woman: mashkūra
culture: On a home visit the greetings go back and forth: how are you, hope you're well, praise God, God keep you. Answer each one with a formula; nobody expects news yet. Bringing something small, such as sweets or dates, is a usual courtesy.

title: Where did you go last night?
goal: Say where you went, when you got back, and that you didn't go
tip: For “I” in the past the verb ends in -t: rijaʿt (I came back), tiʿabt (I got tired); riḥt (I went) is irregular, so learn it as a word. The same form means “you (a man)”: wēn riḥt? For “didn't”, put ma first: ma riḥt (I didn't go).
grammar: Past tense: I and you (a man) -t; ma + past
dialogue: Where did you go last night?
I went to the mall with my mates.
Nice. And when did you get back?
And you didn't go to uni this morning?
No, I didn't. I was really tired.
items: I went / you went (to a man)
where did you go? (to a man)
I came back / you came back (to a man)
I got tired / you got tired (to a man)
to a woman: tiʿabti (تعبتي); tiʿabt wāyid = I was really tired; also “I felt unwell”

title: Did you have coffee?
goal: Chat with Maryam about the morning: when you got in and what you've done
tip: To a woman, “you” in the past adds -ti: wiṣalti? (did you get in?), shirabti? (did you have a drink?). To a man it's the same as “I”: wiṣalt can mean “I arrived” or “you (a man) arrived”.
dialogue: صباح الخير يا مريم! متى وصلتي؟
ṣabāḥ il-khēr yā Maryam! mita wiṣalti?
Good morning, Maryam! When did you get in?
ṣabāḥ in-nūr. wiṣalt il-ḥīn. w inta?
Good morning. I've just got in. And you?
I got in at eight. Have you had a coffee?
لا، ما شربت. كتبت الإيميل حق المدير؟
la, ma shirabt. kitabt il-īmēl ḥagg il-mudīr?
No, I haven't. Did you write the email to the manager?
Yes, I did. Shall we go for a coffee?
items: I arrived / you arrived (to a man)
when did you get here? (to a woman)
I drank / you drank (to a man)
I didn't drink, I haven't had (one)
I wrote / you wrote (to a man)
yalla nishrab gahwa? = shall we have a coffee?

title: He went, she went
goal: Ask a colleague where people are and say where they went
tip: “He” is the bare verb: wiṣal (he arrived), rāḥ (he went). “She” adds -at. In verbs like wiṣal the vowel before it drops: wiṣlat, rijʿat; rāḥ just adds it: rāḥat. In writing wiṣlat (وصلت) looks like wiṣalt (I arrived): the sentence tells you which.
grammar: Past tense: he (no ending) and she (-at)
dialogue: هيه، وصل الصبح، بس طلع قبل شوي
hē, wiṣal iṣ-ṣubḥ, bas ṭilaʿ gabil shwayy
Yes, he got in this morning, but he went out a moment ago.
Where did he go? And Maryam?
ما أدري. ومريم رجعت البيت، تعبت شوي
ma adri. w Maryam rijʿat il-bēt, tiʿbat shwayy
I don't know. And Maryam went home, she wasn't feeling well.
items: he came back, he went back
she: rijʿat (رجعت); rijʿat il-bēt = she went home, no word for “to”
I hope she's OK (when someone is ill)
about a man: salāmtah; reply: allāh ysallmak

title: We went to the beach
goal: Tell Maryam where you and Sēf went and when you got home
tip: “We” adds -na: riḥna (we went), wiṣalna (we arrived), ṭilaʿna (we went out). ma works the same: ma riḥna (we didn't go). For “Sēf and I”, Gulf puts ana first: ana w Sēf.
dialogue: Did you go out last night?
Yes, Sēf and I went out.
We went to the beach, for the first time!
Lovely! And when did you get back?
We got home late, at one.
items: I went out / you went out (to a man)
a woman: mitʼakhkhra; wiṣalna mitʼakhkhir = we got there late
